title: Stanford CS153 Frontier Systems | Amit Jain from Luma AI on Unified Intelligence Systems
transcriptText:
Welcome, gang, to
week 3 of CS153.
We have today with us
Amit Jain from Luma.
Thank you for joining us, Amit.
Thanks for having me.
OK.
[APPLAUSE]
Amit is going to be talking
to us today about unified
intelligence systems.
You're going to be hearing
a lot more about this.
I think it's a very
relevant follow-up
to the visual
intelligence systems
lecture we had last
week from Andy Blattman
at Black Forest Labs.
Quick recap on the
class and today,
we're going to talk about Amit.
And today we're going to
do a field trip into what
I think is also one of the
most exciting factories working
on how to get work
done, especially
visual and creative work done
in the world called Luma.
But before that,
why don't we start
by talking about
Amit a little bit?
I had the privilege to get to
Amit a few years ago, when he
was still an engineer at Apple.
And I was at
Discord at the time.
And I got an email
from Amit saying, hey,
I heard you have a
bunch of 3D data.
Can I have it?
[CHUCKLES]
I remember that.
And I said, no, you
can't, because Discord
had acquired the data.
But I started asking
why he needed the data.
If you guys remember, I covered
this in our first lecture.
But Ubiquity6, the company I
started about a decade ago,
was a 3D computer
vision mapping company.
And we had millions of people
around the world who were
capturing the world in 3D using
their smartphones and all that
data-- we had terabytes of data
that were 3D representations
of the world that we'd
reconstructed from 2D images.
And Amit said, well, I want
to build a 3D service that is
generative.
I want to allow people to
create the same kinds of meshes
and point clouds and 3D
representations of spaces
but through generative models,
because that's where the world
is going.
And I got interested
because I agreed with him,
and he was ahead of the curve.
And so I had a chance to
invest as an Angel Investor
at the time.
And then a few years
later, I had a chance
to partner with
Amit again at a16z
when I was a general partner.
And thank you for letting
me lead your Series--
--B.
Yeah.
Amit was also one of
the first customers
of the a16z compute program
called Oxygen and actually
helped name Oxygen as well.
I think the quote
was, he said something
like, if we don't have
compute on day one,
can't really breathe.
Yeah.
So tell us a little
bit about what Luma is.
And what were the dots that
led from the insight at Apple
that generative modeling was
the future that led here?
My background, very
briefly-- so at Apple,
I was working on first the
LiDAR systems that actually now
is on our iPhones.
This was called the Jasper
sensor, if any of you
are familiar.
And we were trying
to actually build
what comes after the camera.
The sensor was built now.
I can talk about it because the
project is no more for the car,
which was called Titan.
And we started to
work on Vision Pro
after that because the
car project got canceled,
and the Vision Pro had a
bunch of leaders on it.
And during that work, it
started to become obvious
that, OK, the computers
of the future, we
still don't what
they will look like.
Maybe they will
have AI or what not.
The computers of the future will
need very different interfaces,
will need very
different kind of media,
and will need very
different kind
of ways of actually capturing
and creating and building
those things into the system.
So in 2020, at Apple, we started
exploring generative models.
And think about it.
It's 2020 so before language
model scaling was known
to be working and before--
actually, it was before
DALL-E. But NeRF had already
come out from Matthew
Tancik from Berkeley.
So we started to explore
those generative systems,
and that led me to
thinking that, OK,
if language scaling is working,
and here is a method where
differentiable 3D is possible,
what would happen if all
of these things are
combined together?
That would basically mean
you have the full footprint
of every observation
in the universe,
and you will be able to
differentiably learn about them.
If you can differentiably
learn about them,
you can understand them.
And then finally, you
can generate them.
So that was the genesis of Luma.
And at that time, because
of the pedigree we had,
3D seemed like the most
logical way of going forward
because first of all, 3D has a
lot more information than images
do.
Naively, we assumed at the time
3D has a lot more information
than videos do as well and that
4D would be very easy to capture
and scale.
But again, I say
naively, because,
as you will learn
in a few seconds,
that that was a bad assumption.
But that's where we started
with the idea of building
what we now call
a world simulator.
At that time, it was
just like, all right,
if you can learn this
and generate this,
we would have something
that would allow us
world understanding.
And you talked about you said
this phrase, which is important.
"Learn the world in a
differentiable manner."
What does that mean?
Right, so I mean, I'm
sure you guys are all
familiar with how transformers
work and how AI models work.
Differentiable means you can
put it in a training loop,
and you can have a loss function
that can be then iteratively
optimized.
So differentiable
allows you to do that.
If the function is
not differentiable,
then you really can't do
gradient descent on it.
And if you can't do
gradient descent on it,
then deep learning doesn't work.
So the tools that we have for
this era for this generation
is basically compute
and gradient descent.
And yes, transformers
are things that
are very, very well susceptible
to gradient descent.
But the actual
thing underneath it
is gradient descent and compute.
So how can we take a lot
of data, a lot of compute,
and gradient descent and produce
something useful out of it?
Differentiability is the core
characteristic of that problem,
those problems, basically.
Yep, that's helpful.
Can you just connect
the dots on what
that insight led to then
what do was doing today?
So when we started the
company, the idea was,
we will capture an
ungodly amount of 3D data,
build a flywheel that allows
people to capture that
and for us to be able to use it
and then build world simulation
systems with it.
So we released an app, which
is called Luma 3D Capture.
It actually was
very, very popular
because, one, the results
were really, really great.
It was for the first time
that NeRF and Gaussian
Splats were productionized.
And Matthew, he joined
our team actually
to really push
forward the frontier
of that part of the world.
But very soon, we realized
that it doesn't matter
how many people use the app.
It will never reach
the scale that
was necessary to learn
enough about the universe.
Why is that?
Because think about it.
The number of people that are
riding on the internet that
are taking photos on the
internet, that are capturing
videos on the internet,
substantially outpaces anything
one company can
actually distribute.
Also, there's decades
and decades and decades
of that information that
is already available.
So it's all about data.
You can make the case that this
particular modality of data
is better for learning
versus this or versus that.
It really doesn't matter.
That's a moot point
because you're running
against the physics of scale.
So wherever there
is scale in data,
that's the only thing
that's going to work.
And you have to
design the algorithms
around where the data is,
not the other way around.
You come up with some
pristine algorithm,
but you don't have any data.
Then what's the point?
Robotics is coming up
against this problem
right now where,
all right, we're
going to build these
action systems.
But, well, where
is the action data?
There's no internet
of action data.
You can have huge labs
in China and India
and Vietnam and everywhere
gathering this data,
but the scale is
really not comparable.
So you have to just design
the systems around data,
so that's what we learned.
So in 2023, after
that realization
and after NVIDIA Hopper
architecture was announced,
we started to build the
foundations of generative video
because video is
three dimensional.
It has two dimensions of space
and one dimension of time.
And human brain actually learns
about 3D representation through
that time proxy.
So when Hopper architecture
came about, we started to think,
all right, it might be possible
actually to learn video
and to learn the world
representation through video.
So in 2023, Jiaming joined us.
Jiaming was at
NVIDIA at that point.
He's a Stanford grad.
And a few other people
from Stanford and Berkeley
started to join the company
with this idea of, all right,
let's learn from video.
And we started to build
that infrastructure.
And in March 2024, we
released the first video model
that was called Dream Machine.
And in the first three
weeks, four weeks,
actually, we got up
to 6 million users
from that because people had
never seen generative video.
So it was announced but never
released, so people had never
experienced it.
So people really wanted
to actually try that out.
So we started with
video at that point.
And then we have had the similar
realization again in 2025,
early 2025-- it's just
like annual cycles now--
that just video is not
enough, because video is good.
But it doesn't pair human logic.
It doesn't pair why
an event is important.
What is the sequence of events,
and what does that actually
lead to?
Just having language
models in the middle
that are being used for
embedding is not sufficient.
You need unified intelligence.
So that's where we are now.
These are the dots.
Well, yeah, so this is not the
first time the class has heard
that when you
close the loop, you
have to evolve the mid-training,
the post-training pipeline,
the interface.
And so can we spend a
little bit of time--
so I don't think it's
a surprise for people
to hear that there was an
iterative loop every year as you
got more and more
data from customers.
But can we talk a little
bit about that first--
the final projects for
the class this time
are the one-person
frontier lab, where
they're going to
be bootstrapping
their own flywheels.
That's pretty cool.
And before, I remember
how nerve wracking it
was for you and
for the team when
you had the realization
that video was going
to be the future, but you
didn't have a video model
out in the world yet.
And you didn't have a
state of the art system
to start collecting that
context feedback loop.

back in time, time travel
to the launch of
Dream Machine 1.
Can you just tell
folks how you went
about kickstarting
or bootstrapping
the video flywheel at Luma?
So I think the core
problem that you
want to think about,
whenever you're
building these really,
really large systems,
they have a wild distribution.
Even if you're talking
about language models,
well, they have all of language
models, language model data.
And what is good?
What is bad?
So you want to think
about, OK, from this really
raw distribution I
get from pre-training,
how do I get to a model
that humans can use?
And what humans find useful
is a very narrow band
within that distribution,
and that narrow band is not
a predictable linear band.
It's just pockets of greatness
that humans think are great.
Some other species might
find it very different.
But we have our own aesthetics.
We have our own use cases.
We have our own value systems.
So we find those
distributions valuable.
So now the question
becomes, how do you find
or how do you basically get that
distribution out of the model?
So we started to think
about that problem.
And with Dream Machine,
because there were so
many users that were using the
model, the question became,
all right, can we learn
something about that?
And preference or
preference feedback--
at that time, by the
way, SFT was just
started to being thought about.
RLHF was the hard
thing where people
were thinking about, all
right, human feedback loops.
So we built a system where are
videos that people were liking
and people were
downloading, we considered
that to be a signal
of, all right,
this is something
that people prefer.
It was not 100% accurate,
because some people
were downloading really
bad videos as a showcase
of how bad I is at video.
So our model also
learned a lot of that.
So we had to then build
systems for humans
to be able to go and
filter out people we pay.
So then it started to emerge
what a frontier lab actually
looks like.
A frontier lab has
these components
of data, these components
of compute and algorithm,
but it also has huge parts of
what we call skills and trainers
and tutors and people who are
doing the labeling of data
and all of these systems.
If you don't have that, then
it's actually not complete.
And a part of that is also
the product you build.
Can the product actually
give you enough information
to make sure that the next model
is better than the previous one?
And hence, the
experience is better,
and hence, more
people will use it,
and hence, you'll get more data
from it about this preference
of human distribution.
And can you make the next
model actually better?
So I mean, it took
us a long time
to learn actually how
to gather that feedback.
And then now the system we
have in the latest Luma agent
system--
ungodly amount of
feedback actually we
get from what people are doing.
Every interaction that
is there we learn from,
whether they like it or dislike
it, in what way they like it,
what way do they dislike it,
whether the full chain of
thought that the model produced
and the full chain of work
that the model produced is any
good, which elements of that
is not good.
And then that's how you actually
start to get good at it.
Well, why don't we
do a double click
on how that actually works.
So to remind everybody about the
field trip we're about to take,
this is the very basic standard
AI factory we've talked about,
frontier AI pipeline.
We've got pre-training,
mid-training,
and then we have
post-training and deployment.
And so today, we're going to
hear a little bit from Amit
on how the Luma
version of this works.
Why don't you go
ahead and just talk us
through what's actually going
on under the hood at Luma.
Absolutely.
So let me talk about what
is informing the design
decisions for our architecture
and for our models.
Currently, we're
seeing huge amount
of alpha coming from
language models being
used for adjacent
tasks like coding,
for adjacent tasks
like system design
and those kind of processes.
But when we start
to think about tasks
that require more context than
what is available in text,
so creative work--
huge amount of things, a
huge amount of information
that is in visual domain,
huge amount of information
in auditory domain, actually,
a huge amount of information
in the trace of how you
arrived at the final output,
that when we think
about robotics,
you can definitely start to
build a robotic system just
based on text models
or VLMs or VLAs
that people are
starting to do now.
But they will not
generalize just the same way
that autonomy--
autonomous driving
didn't generalize
until people started to build
full end-to-end systems that
had language, that had video,
that had all the control
signals, all of these
things in there.
So that's the problem
we are coming up with,
that the real world is way
more complicated than coding.
I mean, coding is a
really valuable task,
but not everything
can be done in coding.
Otherwise, programmers
would be the only profession
that would be left.
And now they're also
endangered species, actually.
But--
I'm not sure that's true, but
I understand your point, yeah.
As a programmer, it's
really fun, actually.
Well, the job has
evolved, for sure,
to become a trainer
and a tutor, yeah.
It's a really fun
time to be that way.
I started coding when I
was 13 years old in order
to build simulation
systems, in order to do--
so my background is in
physics, and in order
to actually build simulation
systems for electromagnetism
and those kinds of things to
see how these systems behave.
That's when I learned
to start coding.
And even at that point, it was
really obvious that I cannot
teach those systems
from any observations.
We can write the code, but
that is like approximations
that we have in our models
or in our equations.
But we can't actually teach
those models from any data.
So all of this is informing
how we build our systems.
So even early on, we
started to think about, OK,
in our pre-training, how can
we learn from all of video,
all of images, and all of text?
It's a really hard problem
because they're really
different modalities,
and they're
expressed very differently.
If you think about the
encoding of these modalities,
text is discrete.
And text performs the
best when you encode it
in a discrete manner.
At least that is
understanding today.
Video is somewhere in
between, and audio and images
are best performed
in continuous space.
So our factory, as you call it,
is built around this idea of,
how do we learn jointly
from all of these systems?
In 2025, these were
disparate towers
that we built, language tower,
image tower, video tower,
audio tower.
And then we would
unify them together
using just some
fusion techniques
so that they will do better.
If you look at the work from
Andy's lab, stable diffusion,
those kind of
things, that's what
it does as well, where you
have a tiny little language
component.

embeddings from that
to be able to understand
the human instructions.
It was just not sufficient.
So when we talk
to our customers,
when they try to use
our system, so where
are systems being
used, for instance?
Currently, large studios.
So actually, I'm very,
very, very excited
about a new show that is
coming out on Prime Video.
The trailer is out.
It's called Old Stories.
It's about Moses.
So Sir Ben Kingsley
is the star of it.
It's a proper production.
It's not an AI video.

produced using Luma agents.

really high, intense situations
where they want to
be able to model
the whole world and the physics
of the world and light and fluid
and interactions and all
of these kind of things.
Now, when you do
that, it's just not
sufficient to build an image
model or a video model.

understands time and causality
and language.

proper instructions.
OK, well, this looks good.

had, this particular thing right
here?
How do you express
that instruction?
In time, when this person
actually walks through the door,
the whole scene explodes.
What does walking through
the door actually mean?
When the person walks
through the door,
what does this explosion

these kind of problems--
and this is a very,
very, very big market.

their job.

actually are employed
in this industry, so about
two times, three times
by estimation of coders.

the physics of the real
world into computers.

systems for them.

do that, you want
to build what we are now
calling unified models that
have the same understanding
and intelligence of a language
model, that can follow
context, that can remember,
and the physical understanding
and the world model
understanding of video
models and image models.

that is what the things we want
to produce.

models got really good, what

to do the full work end to end.

why can't it make

why can't it actually

training.

trillion parameter

learning and continual learning

when you started

critical context

war at the moment.

from what users

visual artifacts

projects.

Models, you start to
